questions.question: What problem do consensus algorithms solve in distributed systems?

options.text: Optimizing network bandwidth utilization across nodes
Getting multiple nodes to agree on a single value despite failures
Distributing computational load evenly across cluster members
Encrypting communication between distributed components

questions.explanation: Consensus algorithms ensure distributed nodes agree on values (leader election, transaction ordering, configuration changes) even when some nodes fail or messages are delayed. This is the fundamental coordination problem in distributed systems. Without consensus, you cannot build reliable distributed databases, configuration stores, or coordination services. The FLP impossibility result (Fischer, Lynch, Paterson 1985) proves that deterministic consensus is impossible with even one faulty process in an asynchronous system, which is why practical algorithms use timeouts and randomization.

questions.question: Which are well-known consensus algorithms? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: Paxos (Lamport, 1989)
Raft (Ongaro & Ousterhout, 2014)
Consistent Hashing (Karger et al., 1997)
Zab (ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast)

questions.explanation: Paxos, Raft, and Zab are consensus algorithms for distributed agreement. Paxos is the foundational algorithm (used in Google Chubby, Spanner). Raft was designed for understandability (used in etcd, Consul, CockroachDB). Zab is ZooKeeper's protocol (used in Kafka, Hadoop). Consistent hashing is a data distribution algorithm, not a consensus protocol. It solves a different problem: how to distribute data across nodes, not how to get nodes to agree on values.

questions.question: Why was Raft designed as an alternative to Paxos?

options.text: Paxos has fundamental correctness issues that Raft fixes
Raft provides stronger consistency guarantees than Paxos
Raft is designed to be more understandable and easier to implement correctly
Paxos cannot handle more than three nodes in a cluster

questions.explanation: Raft was explicitly designed for understandability. Paxos is notoriously difficult to understand and implement correctly. Leslie Lamport's original Paxos paper used a Greek parliament metaphor that confused readers. Raft achieves equivalent guarantees with a clearer structure: distinct phases for leader election, log replication, and safety. The Raft paper includes a user study showing Raft is significantly easier to understand. This matters because consensus bugs can cause data loss or corruption. Understandability enables correct implementation.

questions.question: In Raft, what happens when the leader fails?

options.text: The system stops accepting writes until an administrator intervenes
Followers detect the timeout and automatically elect a new leader
The most recently updated follower automatically becomes leader
A random follower is selected as leader without election

questions.explanation: Raft followers have randomized election timeouts. When they do not hear from the leader within the timeout, they become candidates and request votes from other nodes. A candidate with majority votes becomes the new leader. This is fully automatic with no human intervention required. The randomized timeouts prevent split votes where multiple candidates tie. etcd clusters typically recover from leader failure in 1-2 seconds. The election timeout is configurable but typically 150-300ms.

questions.question: What is a 'quorum' in consensus algorithms?

options.text: The total number of nodes in the cluster
The minimum number of nodes that must agree for a decision to be valid
The designated leader node that coordinates consensus
A backup node that takes over during failures

questions.explanation: Quorum is the minimum nodes needed to make progress, typically a majority (N/2 + 1). This ensures any two quorums overlap by at least one node, preventing conflicting decisions. A 5-node cluster needs 3 nodes to agree. The overlap guarantee is crucial: if quorum Q1 decided value X and quorum Q2 decides value Y, at least one node was in both quorums and would reject the conflicting decision. This is the mathematical foundation of consensus safety.

questions.question: A Raft cluster has 5 nodes. How many node failures can it tolerate while still making progress?

options.text: 1 node (must maintain 80% availability)
2 nodes (majority of 3 can still form quorum)
3 nodes (any 2 nodes can elect a leader)
4 nodes (single node can operate independently)

questions.explanation: With 5 nodes, quorum is 3 (majority). The cluster can tolerate 2 failures and still have 3 nodes to form quorum. With 3 failures, only 2 nodes remain, which is not enough for quorum. This is why production clusters use odd numbers: 3 nodes tolerates 1 failure, 5 tolerates 2, 7 tolerates 3. The formula: a cluster of N nodes tolerates (N-1)/2 failures. Kubernetes etcd clusters typically use 3 or 5 nodes depending on availability requirements.

questions.question: What is the 'split-brain' problem in distributed systems?

options.text: When a node's CPU becomes overloaded processing requests
When two network partitions each believe they are the authoritative cluster
When memory is fragmented across distributed nodes
When network latency causes request timeouts

questions.explanation: Split-brain occurs when a network partition creates two groups, each electing its own leader and accepting writes independently. This causes data divergence and potential data loss when the partition heals. Quorum-based consensus prevents this because only the majority partition can achieve quorum and operate. The minority partition cannot elect a leader or commit writes. This is why consensus algorithms require majority agreement, not just any subset of nodes.

questions.question: Why do consensus algorithms typically require an odd number of nodes?

options.text: Even numbers cause mathematical errors in quorum calculations
Odd numbers ensure a clear majority exists and avoid tie situations
Network protocols require odd-numbered addressing
Storage systems perform better with odd node counts

questions.explanation: With even nodes (e.g., 4), a 2-2 split has no majority, and both partitions are stuck. With odd nodes (e.g., 5), one partition always has majority (at least 3). Odd numbers also maximize fault tolerance per node: 4 nodes still need 3 for quorum (same as 3 nodes), so the 4th node adds cost without improving fault tolerance. The recommendation: use 3 nodes for development/small deployments, 5 for production requiring higher availability, 7 for critical systems.

questions.question: Can consensus algorithms make progress during network partitions if a majority of nodes are in one partition?

options.text: No, all nodes must be reachable for consensus to work
Yes, the majority partition can continue; the minority partition cannot
Yes, both partitions continue independently and merge later
No, partitions always cause complete system unavailability

questions.explanation: The majority partition can form quorum and continue operating normally, electing leaders and committing writes. The minority partition cannot make progress because it cannot achieve quorum, but it does not cause split-brain. This is the CP tradeoff in CAP theorem terms: consistency is preserved (no conflicting writes), but availability is sacrificed in the minority partition. When the partition heals, minority nodes catch up from the majority's log.

questions.question: Which systems use consensus algorithms internally? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: etcd (Kubernetes configuration store)
Apache ZooKeeper (distributed coordination)
Redis in single-node mode
CockroachDB (distributed SQL database)

questions.explanation: etcd uses Raft for distributed consensus. ZooKeeper uses Zab (ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast). CockroachDB uses Raft for distributed transactions across ranges. Single-node Redis does not need consensus because there is only one node. Consensus is specifically for coordinating multiple nodes. When Redis is used in cluster mode with replication, it uses a simpler primary-replica model, not full consensus, which is why Redis Cluster can have data loss during failover.

questions.question: What is the main performance cost of consensus algorithms?

options.text: High memory usage for storing consensus state
Latency from requiring multiple nodes to acknowledge writes before confirming
CPU-intensive cryptographic operations for message signing
Large disk storage for consensus logs

questions.explanation: Consensus requires waiting for quorum acknowledgment before confirming writes. This adds network round-trip latency, typically 1-10ms within a datacenter, 50-200ms across regions. The tradeoff is consistency and fault tolerance for write latency. Read latency can be lower if reads are served from the leader or if linearizable reads are not required. Google Spanner accepts this latency cost for global strong consistency. Systems that cannot tolerate this latency often choose eventual consistency instead.

questions.question: In Paxos, what are the three roles nodes can play?

options.text: Leader, Follower, Candidate
Proposer, Acceptor, Learner
Primary, Secondary, Arbiter
Coordinator, Participant, Observer

questions.explanation: Paxos defines Proposers (propose values), Acceptors (vote on proposals and form quorums), and Learners (learn decided values and can serve reads). A single node can play multiple roles simultaneously. This separation of concerns is elegant but makes Paxos harder to understand. Raft simplified this to Leader (combines proposer and primary acceptor), Follower (acceptor and learner), and Candidate (during elections). The Raft simplification sacrifices some flexibility for understandability.
